segments.text: This video will review how to perform an ultrasound guided tibial nerve block for regional anesthesia.
The tibial nerve block provides regional anesthesia primarily to the bottom of the foot.
This is especially useful in the emergency department for pain control
or for foreign body exploration of the bottom of the foot.
It can be used for calcaneal fracture pain control.
These are the essential elements to perform an ultrasound guided tibial nerve block.
Obtain consent from your patient before the procedure.
Parton and risks include bleeding and pain, infection, damage to local structures, especially
the tubular nerve and its branches.
Position the patient's supine and externally rotate their leg.
You may support their leg with a blanket, a rolled-up towel, or a pillow underneath their
knee.
Stand on the posterior aspect of their leg with the ultrasound across from you.
The tubular nerve is found on the medial aspect of the lower extremity, identify the medial
maliolis. Place the ultrasound probe just proximal to the medial maliolis and a short axis orientation.
Slide the probe's cephalad and identify several structures, including the tibial artery and vein.
The bundle of grapes that forms the tibial nerve is posterior to these vascular structures.
You can utilize color doppler ultrasound to identify the vascular structures.
Draw up your anesthetic of choice using the 18 gauge needle into your preferred syringe.
We generally recommend about 10ccs of anesthetic.
Prepare the skin over your intended site with chlorhexanine.
Cover the ultrasound with a sterile probe cover and apply sterile gel.
Identify the tibial nerve as described before by placing the linear ultrasound probe short axis to the nerve.
Insert the blocking needle from posterior to medial.
Focus on getting the needle underneath the probe.
You don't need to look at the ultrasound screen, just get the needle underneath the probe
and then visualize the needle tip on the ultrasound screen.
Advanced the ultrasound needle above the nerve and inject your anesthetic.
Visualize the needle tip the entire time and ensure that you are not injecting directly into
the nerve.
Aim to inject above and below the nerve, which creates a halo effect, avoid injecting directly
into the tubular artery or the vein, allow 10 to 15 minutes for the anesthetic to take
effect and monitor for signs of local anesthetic toxicity including perioral, numbness and tingling,
dizziness, shortness of breath, chest pain and more.
